claims.text: Introducing an intermediate thermal dwell into a rapid heating/cooling process enhances atomic interdiffusion.
Enhanced interdiffusion during the dwell promotes formation of a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
An intermediate dwell suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation.
An intermediate dwell suppresses abnormal or non-uniform particle morphology.
Limited atomic mobility during ultra-rapid processing causes phase separation, elemental segregation, and non-uniform morphology in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
A moderated thermal ramp with an optimized intermediate dwell allows greater diffusion before quenching than immediate rapid heating and cooling.
For systems containing more than five elements, high mixing entropy can favor single-phase nanoparticle formation.
Rapid kinetic processing typically produces segregation and high thermal-decomposition thresholds in the applicable compositional range.
Enhanced interdiffusion reduces kinetic barriers and produces a more uniform elemental distribution.
A more uniform elemental distribution stabilizes the solid-solution structure and minimizes defects.
The dwell gives atoms enough time to equilibrate locally, reducing transient concentration gradients and secondary-phase nucleation.
Controlled diffusion during the dwell counteracts kinetic trapping caused by ultra-fast thermal processing.
Relative to immediate quenching, dwell-treated nanoparticles will have greater phase homogeneity and a single solid-solution crystal structure.
Dwell-treated nanoparticles will have reduced elemental segregation and more uniform morphology.
Dwell-treated nanoparticles will exhibit lower lattice strain.
Dwell-treated nanoparticles will exhibit more controlled thermal-decomposition behavior.
The hypothesis may fail where the thermodynamic driving force for segregation is too strong.
An excessively long or high-temperature dwell may cause particle growth, agglomeration, or a different phase transition.
